sermon:
A man writes from a Roman cell, and the first thing he does is remember someone's grandmother. Not his charges. Not his appeal. He thinks about Lois and Eunice, two women who carried a faith down three generations until it landed in a young pastor named Timothy. Paul is in chains, the winter is coming, and he is writing a letter to a frightened man.

That is the situation. Timothy is real, the gift in him is real, and so is the fear that has begun to bank the fire down to coals.

**The gift was given, and it was fading.**

Paul does not tell Timothy to manufacture something he lacks. He tells him to stir up what is already there. "For this reason I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God, which is in you through the laying on of my hands" (2 Timothy 1:6). The word is a kitchen word, the work of a man crouched over a hearth, blowing on embers until they catch again. The gift had not died. It had dimmed. And a dimming gift in a man who has stopped tending it is the most common tragedy in the church, and the quietest.

What had dimmed it was fear. We do not like to say that about ourselves. We call it discretion, or prudence, or knowing the room. But Paul names it: "for God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control" (2 Timothy 1:7). The fear was real. The opposition was real. Some had already turned away. Phygelus and Hermogenes are named, not for their crimes, but for their absence. They left. And Timothy, watching men he respected walk away from a chained apostle, began to wonder if silence was safer.

I have done this. I have felt the gift in me and chosen not to blow on it, because the room was cold and the cost was clear. We call it being careful. God calls it a spirit that did not come from Him.

**The cure for shame is not nerve but the gospel itself.**

Paul does not answer Timothy's fear with a motivational speech. He answers it with Christ. "Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony about our Lord, nor of me his prisoner, but share in suffering for the gospel by the power of God" (2 Timothy 1:8). The shame is real, so Paul puts something heavier on the other side of the scale. He puts a Savior "who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel" (2 Timothy 1:10).

That is the engine of the whole letter. A man can speak of dying without flinching because death has already been broken. Paul is not ashamed, "for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me" (2 Timothy 1:12). Notice the order. The deposit Timothy must guard is finally guarded by the One Timothy trusts. We keep the gospel because the gospel keeps us.

And then, almost tenderly, Paul names a man who got it right. Onesiphorus was not ashamed of Paul's chains. He searched the city of Rome until he found the prisoner, and he refreshed him. While the impressive men disappeared, an ordinary man went looking for a chained apostle in a hostile city. That is what fanning the flame looks like in the body. It looks like someone refusing to be embarrassed by you when you are at your weakest.

**The deposit is not yours to bury.**

The charge lands twice. "Follow the pattern of the sound words that you have heard from me... By the Holy Spirit who dwells within us, guard the good deposit entrusted to you" (2 Timothy 1:13-14). The gospel is a deposit. It was handed to you intact, and you do not get to improve it, soften it, or sit on it until the climate warms. You guard it. And you guard it not by your own grip, which fails, but by the Spirit who lives in you.

Here is the Christ connection, and it is the spine of everything. Paul can be unashamed in a cell because Jesus was not ashamed of a cross. The Savior who brought life out of a tomb is able to guard the deposit, guard the man, and light the fire again in a pastor who had let it cool. Your nerve will fail. His faithfulness will not.

So blow on the coals. The gift is still in there. The Spirit is still in you. And the One who entrusted you the gospel is well able to keep both you and it.

Guard the deposit. Stop being ashamed.

Hand a soldier a second job and watch what happens to the first one. He misses formation. He is somewhere across town settling a dispute that was never his to settle, and when the line is tested he is not on it. Paul reaches for that picture, and two others, because he is trying to tell a tired young pastor how a man holds up under a weight he is not allowed to put down.

The letter has moved from the hearth to the field. Chapter one was about a flame that needed tending. Chapter two is about a load that has to be carried, and carried a particular way.

**Strength comes before strain, and the strength is grace.**

The opening is not what you expect from a man in chains. "You then, my child, be strengthened by the grace that is in Christ Jesus" (2 Timothy 2:1). Notice he does not say be strengthened by your discipline, or your stamina, or your sincerity. The strength is grace, and it is in Christ, which means it is supplied from outside the exhausted pastor, not squeezed out of him.

Then comes the chain of custody for the gospel. "What you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses entrust to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also" (2 Timothy 2:2). Count the generations: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, others also. Four links in one sentence. The gospel does not survive by being defended once. It survives by being handed forward, again and again, to people reliable enough to hand it forward again. A pastor who only preaches and never entrusts is the last link in a chain he was supposed to extend.

I feel the rebuke. It is easier to do the work than to give it away. Entrusting it to faithful men means trusting men who will do it differently than I would, and slower, and that is its own small death of pride.

**Three pictures of a man who does not quit.**

Then the three images. The soldier: "No soldier gets entangled in civilian pursuits, since his aim is to please the one who enlisted him" (2 Timothy 2:4). The danger is not opposition. The danger is entanglement, the slow accumulation of good things that are not your assignment, until you are too busy to fight. The athlete: "an athlete is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules" (2 Timothy 2:5). There is no shortcut to the crown. You run the actual race, by the actual rules, or you do not win, however hard you ran outside the lane.

And the farmer: "It is the hard-working farmer who ought to have the first share of the crops" (2 Timothy 2:6). The farmer's reward is at the far end of a season of unglamorous labor in the dirt before anything green appears. Soldier, athlete, farmer. Single-mindedness, integrity, patience. None of them avoid hardship. All of them get the reward on the other side of it.

The glue under all three is one line: "Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, the offspring of David" (2 Timothy 2:8). The reason a man endures is a risen Lord. Paul suffers, "bound with chains as a criminal. But the word of God is not bound" (2 Timothy 2:9). They can chain the preacher. They cannot chain the message. That is the freedom that lets a man in a cell tell a free man to keep going.

**Be the kind of vessel the Master can use.**

The chapter turns toward the church and its quarrels. There are men teaching that the resurrection is already past, and "their talk will spread like gangrene" (2 Timothy 2:17). Against that, Paul lays a foundation that holds: "The Lord knows those who are his," and "Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity" (2 Timothy 2:19).

Then the test of a useful vessel: "if anyone cleanses himself from what is dishonorable, he will be a vessel for honorable use, set apart as holy, useful to the master of the house" (2 Timothy 2:21). Usefulness is not about gifting. It is about cleanness. And the servant of the Lord must not be quarrelsome but kind, "correcting his opponents with gentleness" (2 Timothy 2:24-25), because the goal is not to win the argument but to win the person back from the snare.

Here is the Christ connection. The Master who calls for clean vessels is the One who makes them clean. The grace that strengthens in verse one is the same grace that scrubs the vessel for honorable use. Christ endured His own race to the end and rose, and that risen Christ is both the message we carry and the strength to carry it.

So carry it. Stay in your lane. Stay in the dirt. And hand it forward before you go.

Endure. Entrust it to faithful men.

Read the list slowly and you will recognize the people in it. Lovers of self. Lovers of money. Proud, abusive, ungrateful. Lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God. It reads like a description of a culture in decline, and it is, except for the last clause, which moves the whole thing inside the church door. These people have "the appearance of godliness, but denying its power" (2 Timothy 3:5). They are not outside. They are in the pew, and some of them are in the pulpit.

Paul is preparing Timothy for difficult days, and he is honest about where the difficulty will sit. Not only out there. In here.

**The last days are hard because godliness gets hollowed out.**

"But understand this, that in the last days there will come times of difficulty" (2 Timothy 3:1). The Greek word for difficulty is the same one used elsewhere for the violent men no one could pass on the road. Harsh times. And the harshness is not war or famine first. It is character. The list begins with love aimed the wrong direction, self and money and pleasure where God should be, and it ends with religion that keeps the shape and loses the substance.

That last line should stop every preacher cold. A form of godliness denying its power is not the sin of the irreligious. It is the sin of the church person who has learned the vocabulary, mastered the appearance, and quietly let the engine go cold. "Avoid such people" (2 Timothy 3:5), Paul says, because they are persuasive, and they go after the vulnerable, "creeping into households and capturing weak women" who are "always learning and never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth" (2 Timothy 3:6-7).

I have to ask whether the form has ever outrun the power in me. Whether there have been seasons I kept the appearance and lost the thing it was meant to appear. The honest answer is yes, and the only thing that exposes it is the very Scripture Paul is about to commend.

**Two anchors against the collapse: the people and the page.**

Against all of that, Paul gives Timothy two things to hold. The first is people. "You, however, have followed my teaching, my conduct, my aim in life, my faith, my patience, my love, my steadfastness, my persecutions and sufferings" (2 Timothy 3:10-11). Timothy did not learn the faith from a book alone. He learned it from a man whose life he watched under pressure. And he learned it earlier still from his mother and grandmother. "Continue in what you have learned and have firmly believed, knowing from whom you learned it" (2 Timothy 3:14). From whom. Doctrine arrives through trusted people, and that is not a weakness of the faith. It is how God built it.

Paul is clear-eyed about the cost of that road: "all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted" (2 Timothy 3:12). Not might be. Will be. The hard times do not exempt the faithful. They aim at them.

The second anchor is the page. "From childhood you have been acquainted with the sacred writings, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus" (2 Timothy 3:15). And then the sentence the whole church stands on: "All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work" (2 Timothy 3:16-17).

**Breathed out by God, and therefore enough.**

Breathed out by God. The image is the breath of the Almighty across the words, the same breath that made man a living soul now resting on the page. That is why Scripture can do what it does: teach, reprove, correct, train. It does not only inform. It confronts and rebuilds. And it makes the man of God complete, which means the pastor is not waiting on some further technique to be ready. He is equipped, by the Word, for every good work.

Here is the Christ connection, and it is in the text itself. The sacred writings make us "wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus." The Bible is not an end. It is the instrument that puts us in front of the Savior. When the last days hollow out the form of godliness, the God-breathed Word keeps pointing past itself to the One whose power the hollow religion had denied. The page is anchored because the Christ it preaches is risen.

So when the form is everywhere and the power is rare, go back to the people who taught you and the book that breathes. Continue in it.

Scripture is God-breathed. Continue in it.

Some men dictate a will. Paul, with the cold of a Roman dungeon settling into his bones and the winter coming on, dictates a charge instead. He has asked Timothy to come before winter, and to bring the cloak he left at Troas, and the books. A dying man asking for a coat and his books, and in the same breath laying the heaviest command in the letter on the one he is leaving behind.

This is the end. Paul knows it. "I am already being poured out as a drink offering, and the time of my departure has come" (2 Timothy 4:6). Everything in the letter has been moving toward this charge, and now it lands.

**Preach the word, in season and out.**

He puts Timothy under oath. "I charge you in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who is to judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom: preach the word; be ready in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, and exhort, with complete patience and teaching" (2 Timothy 4:1-2). The charge is given before the Judge and in light of the appearing, which means preaching is never merely a Sunday task. It is done under the eye of Christ and toward the day of Christ.

In season and out of season. When it lands and when it does not. When the room leans in and when it crosses its arms. Paul knows the resistance is coming: "the time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching, but having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions" (2 Timothy 4:3). They will not reject teaching. They will assemble a roster of teachers who tell them what they came to hear. The danger is not an empty church. It is a full one, gathered around a message it selected for comfort.

That is the temptation in my own study every week, to file off the edge that would cost me the room. To scratch the itch instead of preaching the word. Paul will not allow it. "As for you, always be sober-minded, endure suffering, do the work of an evangelist, fulfill your ministry" (2 Timothy 4:5).

**The race was run honestly, and the crown is laid up.**

Then Paul turns and looks at his own end without flinching. "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith" (2 Timothy 4:7). Three verbs, all in the perfect tense, all settled. Not I am fighting, not I hope to finish. Done. He fought, he finished, he kept. This is a man with a sword laid down and a track behind him, and no panic in his voice.

And the reward: "Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will award to me on that Day, and not only to me but also to all who have loved his appearing" (2 Timothy 4:8). Read the last clause again. Not only to Paul. To all who have loved His appearing. The crown is not a prize for apostles. It is laid up for everyone who longed for Christ to come.

The end of the letter is not triumphant in tone. It is human and a little lonely. "Demas, in love with this present world, has deserted me" (2 Timothy 4:10). "At my first defense no one came to stand by me, but all deserted me" (2 Timothy 4:16). And then the line that holds the whole thing up: "But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the message might be fully proclaimed" (2 Timothy 4:17). When the men left, the Lord stood. That is the verse to die on.

**Christ is faithful when the runner falters.**

Here is the Christ connection, and it is the foundation of every confident word in this chapter. The crown is righteousness, and Paul did not earn it by his record. He fought, he finished, he kept, and still the crown comes from "the righteous Judge" who awards it on the basis of the One who remains faithful when we are faithless. Paul can speak of his departure without fear because, as he said at the start, Christ "abolished death and brought life and immortality to light." The race ends at an empty tomb, not a closed one.

So do not preach to the itch. Do not file off the edge. Run the actual race to the actual end, and trust the righteous Judge to crown what His grace produced in you. Paul handed Timothy the gospel and a charge and a coat, and then he went to meet the Lord who stood by him.

Now the line is yours to hold.

I have kept the faith. Preach.
